final_proof:
Let
\[
 H=\left\{x=(x_i)_{i\in I}:x_i\in H_i\text{ and }
        \sum_{i\in I}\|x_i\|_{H_i}^{\,2}<\infty\right\},
\]
where, for a family of nonnegative real numbers, the sum over an arbitrary
index set is defined by
\[
 \sum_{i\in I}a_i:=\sup\left\{\sum_{i\in F}a_i:F\subseteq I
 \text{ finite}\right\}.
\]
This is the Hilbert space direct sum. Its operations are coordinatewise and
its proposed inner product is
\[
 \langle x,y\rangle:=\sum_{i\in I}\langle x_i,y_i\rangle_{H_i}.
\]

We first verify that this expression is meaningful. For every finite
\(F\subseteq I\), finite-dimensional Cauchy--Schwarz (applied to the finite
sequences of real numbers \(\|x_i\|\) and \(\|y_i\|\)) gives
\[
 \sum_{i\in F}|\langle x_i,y_i\rangle|
 \leq \sum_{i\in F}\|x_i\|\,\|y_i\|
 \leq\left(\sum_{i\in F}\|x_i\|^2\right)^{1/2}
      \left(\sum_{i\in F}\|y_i\|^2\right)^{1/2}
 \leq \|x\|\,\|y\|,
\]
where \(\|x\|=(\sum_i\|x_i\|^2)^{1/2}\). Thus the family
\((\langle x_i,y_i\rangle)_{i\in I}\) is absolutely summable (with sums
understood as limits of the net of finite partial sums), so the displayed
inner product exists and satisfies
\(|\langle x,y\rangle|\leq\|x\|\|y\|\). The inner-product axioms follow
coordinatewise from those on the \(H_i\), and
\[
 \langle x,x\rangle=\sum_{i\in I}\|x_i\|^2=\|x\|^2.
\]
In particular it is positive definite. Also, coordinatewise addition and
scalar multiplication preserve membership in \(H\), since
\(\|x_i+y_i\|^2\leq 2\|x_i\|^2+2\|y_i\|^2\). Hence \(H\) is an inner-product
space with the stated norm.

It remains to prove completeness. Let \((x^{(n)})_{n\geq1}\) be a Cauchy
sequence in \(H\), writing \(x^{(n)}=(x_i^{(n)})_{i\in I}\). For each fixed
\(i\),
\[
 \|x_i^{(n)}-x_i^{(m)}\|_{H_i}\leq
 \|x^{(n)}-x^{(m)}\|,
\]
so \((x_i^{(n)})_n\) is Cauchy in the complete space \(H_i\). Let
\(x_i=\lim_n x_i^{(n)}\), and put \(x=(x_i)_{i\in I}\).

Every Cauchy sequence is bounded, so choose \(M<\infty\) with
\(\|x^{(n)}\|\leq M\) for all \(n\). For every finite \(F\subseteq I\),
continuity of the finitely many norms and sums yields
\[
 \sum_{i\in F}\|x_i\|^2
   =\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{i\in F}\|x_i^{(n)}\|^2
   \leq M^2.
\]
Taking the supremum over finite \(F\) shows that
\(\sum_{i\in I}\|x_i\|^2\leq M^2\), and hence \(x\in H\).

Finally, let \(\varepsilon>0\). Choose \(N\) such that
\(\|x^{(n)}-x^{(m)}\|<\varepsilon\) whenever \(m,n\geq N\). Fix
\(n\geq N\). For every finite \(F\subseteq I\), coordinatewise convergence
gives
\[
 \sum_{i\in F}\|x_i^{(n)}-x_i\|^2
 =\lim_{m\to\infty}\sum_{i\in F}
       \|x_i^{(n)}-x_i^{(m)}\|^2
 \leq \varepsilon^2.
\]
Taking the supremum over finite \(F\) gives
\(\|x^{(n)}-x\|\leq\varepsilon\). Therefore \(x^{(n)}\to x\) in \(H\).
Thus every Cauchy sequence in \(H\) converges in \(H\), so the Hilbert space
direct sum is a Hilbert space.
